We do desperately need decentralized chan alternatives. However, the problem with these is ultimately spam and illegal materials.

One proposal I had read a while ago was to use Proof-of-Work as Identity. For background, there was an alternative chan software known as "BitMessage" that used PoW (Proof-of-Work) per post. The problem with this is that it's relatively cheap for a glowing player to spam the boards incessantly. And increasing the PoW difficulty only makes it slightly more expensive for glows, while significantly impacting usability for normal users.

The idea of using PoW as Identity (instead of on a per-post-basis) meant that there would be an initial PoW capital in order to be able to post at all - and this would usually be done by front-end nodes that post with that identity on behalf of their user-base. If one of these front-end nodes became notorious for posting shit/luminescent content, the other nodes could blacklist that identity.

For anyone pondering this point technically, an "identity" doesn't necessarily refer to an individual user, it could be a front-end service that the user is posting through. Essentially, identities just "sign" posts. But this means:

if there was ever a large front-end chan that was signing user's posts and had a notoriously shitty user-base, users who blocked that identity would be blocking the whole user-base of that front-end.

Additionally, there's no guarantee that glows would not be willing to invest in PoW machines to generate these identities - it is still relatively cheap compared to a single employees wage (e.g. 12 computers going at it full pelt would = 1 identity generated per hour).

I recall the author of this proposal mentioning that it might be possible to adjust the PoW (in a similar fashion as other cryptocurrencies) such that only X number of identities could be generated per day. This would make the moderation of fake front-end services manageable in that it would become a sustainable game of whack-a-glow, while also giving a decent indicator of how hard the decentralized chan network was being attacked by shills. I do not know his final thoughts on this aspect and whether he thought it feasible long-term.

His solution for illegal materials was that identities could propagate "revoke" messages to other nodes for messages that they had signed. This is the equivalent of content moderation as we know it - but, unlike current services where the post is outright deleted, whether other nodes choose to abide by the revocation is optional. This actually has an advantage in that other nodes could see which content was being removed - and, if the content was not necessarily illegal, but removed anyway (e.g. Insurance Keys), then there would be good evidence to suggest that that particular identity was compromised.

There is, ultimately, probably not a perfect solution to this problem. I would be keen to hear other proposals.
